regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Aim for lasting cancer control or cure in selected relapsed germ-cell cancer, using high-dose chemotherapy with your own stored stem cells.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Metastatic relapsed/refractory germ-cell tumours. Specialist autologous conditioning pathway.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 5 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 5 mg. Etoposide interferes with an enzyme used to copy and repair DNA. This can stop cancer cells growing and can also lower healthy blood counts.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Carboplatin AUC7 is followed by etoposide 750 mg/m² on days −5, −4 and −3. Your stored stem cells are infused on day 0. Growth-factor injections start on day +1 and continue until the team confirms neutrophil recovery. These day numbers are relative to the stem-cell infusion.
key_points: A specialist conditioning and rescue pathway. The diagram is a relative reference, not an outpatient 28-day cycle or a discharge prediction.

Prescribed anti-sickness treatment is needed across the high-dose days. The local transplant plan includes antiviral and antifungal prevention, mouth care, a proton-pump inhibitor and Pneumocystis pneumonia prevention. Co-trimoxazole starts only after engraftment; the team specifies the stop date. Irradiated cellular blood components are required from one week before conditioning until 12 months after stem-cell infusion.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Treat relapsed or resistant testicular germ-cell cancer, with the possibility of lasting remission in selected patients.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues. Ifosfamide damages cancer-cell DNA. Its breakdown products can also affect the bladder, kidneys and brain. Mesna protects the bladder but does not prevent all kidney or brain effects. Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Paclitaxel is given on day 1. Cisplatin and ifosfamide are given on days 1–5, with bladder-protecting mesna each day. Growth-factor injections start on day 6 until neutrophil recovery under local policy. Four 21-day cycles are planned, subject to consultant review.
key_points: This is NCCP 00602: paclitaxel175 mg/m² day 1, ifosfamide1200 mg/m² and cisplatin20 mg/m² days 1–5. Other published TIP schedules differ.

Cisplatin needs a high-risk anti-sickness plan and prescribed hydration/electrolytes. Ifosfamide needs mesna and adequate fluids. Paclitaxel needs prescribed allergy premedication; reconcile steroid doses with antiemetics. Aprepitant may increase ifosfamide brain toxicity, so pharmacy must review the combination. Growth factor is included from day 6. Retain prescribed mouth care, pain relief and stomach protection.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Reduce the risk of bladder cancer returning or worsening, and treat suitable carcinoma in situ, using local immune treatment.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Intermediate-, high- or very-high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: BCG contains weakened live bacteria. Placing it inside the bladder stimulates a local immune response against abnormal cells. It is not a checkpoint-inhibitor medicine.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: BCG is placed in the bladder once weekly for six weeks. Maintenance uses three weekly instillations at months 3,6 and12 for intermediate-risk disease; high/very-high-risk plans may add months 18,24,30 and36. Your urologist confirms the course according to risk, response, tolerance and supply.
key_points: Live BCG placed inside the bladder. It is not intravenous chemotherapy or PD1/PDL1 checkpoint immunotherapy.

BCG is placed in the bladder once weekly for six weeks. Maintenance uses three weekly instillations at months 3,6 and12 for intermediate-risk disease; high/very-high-risk plans may add months 18,24,30 and36. Your urologist confirms the course according to risk, response, tolerance and supply.

Check symptoms and suitability before each instillation. Cystoscopy with possible biopsy and urine cytology are planned eight weeks after the last BCG dose and regularly afterwards under the urologist’s plan.

Routine anti-sickness or steroid premedication is not usually needed. The source asks for no fluids for four hours before and until two hours after instillation; confirm this is safe with your team, especially with fluid-sensitive conditions. Obtain written instructions for restarting fluids, passing urine, toilet hygiene, spill management and sexual precautions for your exact product.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Help control advanced urothelial cancer with a susceptible FGFR3 alteration after previous PD1/PDL1 treatment.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Unresectable/metastatic urothelial carcinoma with susceptible FGFR3 alteration after at least one PD1/PDL1-containing line in that setting.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Some urothelial cancers use an altered fibroblast growth factor receptor, FGFR3, to drive growth. Erdafitinib blocks this signal. FGFR also helps regulate phosphate handling, explaining why blood phosphate may rise.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: The usual starting dose is8 mg once daily. The team may increase it to9 mg after reviewing phosphate and toxicity on days 14–21. Never change the dose yourself. Treatment is continuous until progression or unacceptable toxicity; the28-day view is only a reference.
key_points: The molecular result must be a susceptible FGFR3 alteration. A general FGFR result or a phosphate rise alone does not prove tumour benefit.

The usual starting dose is8 mg once daily. The team may increase it to9 mg after reviewing phosphate and toxicity on days 14–21. Never change the dose yourself. Treatment is continuous until progression or unacceptable toxicity; the28-day view is only a reference.

Phosphate is checked on days 14–21 and monthly afterwards, more often if elevated. Eye examinations are monthly for the first four months and every three months thereafter; new symptoms need prompt review. Repeat blood count, kidney/liver tests, electrolytes and ECG under the prescribed plan.

High phosphate may need a dietitian-guided phosphate restriction and prescribed phosphate binder. Do not add vitaminD supplements without oncology review. Ask about mouth care, skin/nail care, diarrhoea treatment and dry-eye support. Bring all medicines and supplements for interaction checking.

FGFR also helps regulate phosphate handling, explaining why blood phosphate may rise. FGFR testing selects people whose tumour may respond to this mechanism. Treatment aims to control cancer; scans and symptoms assess benefit separately from phosphate and other safety tests. Other systemic treatment or symptom-directed radiotherapy depends on your individual situation.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Help control advanced urothelial cancer using a targeted chemotherapy-carrying antibody and immune treatment.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: First-line unresectable/metastatic urothelial cancer in adults eligible for platinum chemotherapy.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: An antibody attaches to a protein called nectin-4 and delivers a chemotherapy payload that disrupts cell division. Healthy skin, nerves and other tissues can also be affected. This is not a checkpoint immunotherapy medicine. PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Option 1: enfortumab on days 1 and8 plus pembrolizumab200 mg on day 1, repeating every 21 days. Option 2: enfortumab on days 1,8,22 and29 plus pembrolizumab400 mg on day 1, repeating every 42 days. Your team selects one option. The six-week reference shows two enfortumab blocks; pembrolizumab day 22 applies only to option 1.
key_points: This is the NCCP 00945 advanced-disease combination. It is distinct from28-day enfortumab monotherapy and from perioperative bladder treatment.
